title: A Word for Baruch
summary: In a short personal message dated to the year Baruch first wrote Jeremiah's scroll, God answers Baruch's complaint of grief and exhaustion. God himself is tearing down what he built and uprooting what he planted, so Baruch should not seek great things for himself. What God promises is not success but survival: wherever Baruch goes, he will escape with his life.
story: The book has just recorded Jeremiah's last message in Egypt (chapter 44), and now it steps back about twenty years to the fourth year of Jehoiakim, about 605 BC, the year Baruch wrote the first scroll (36:1-4). The placement is deliberate. After the story of the kingdom's fall and the remnant's flight, the narrative closes with a word to the scribe whose pen preserved it all. In the Greek translation of Jeremiah, which arranges the book differently, this word to Baruch also stands at the end of the main narrative. It works like a signature at the end of a manuscript, and it shows that God cared about the private sorrow of the man who carried the public message. Chapter 46 then begins the oracles concerning the nations.
historical:
Baruch son of Neriah was a scribe, a trained professional who could read and write in a society where many could not. He served as Jeremiah's secretary, legal witness (32:12-16), and public reader (36:8-10), and he was accused of influencing the prophet (43:3). His brother Seraiah son of Neriah was a high official who traveled to Babylon with King Zedekiah (51:59), which suggests that Baruch came from a family with standing at court. His attachment to Jeremiah may have cost him a career of the kind his brother enjoyed.

The fourth year of Jehoiakim, 605 BC, was the year Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt at Carchemish and Babylon became the dominant power in the region. For a young scribe, the future may have looked full of opportunity. Instead, Baruch found himself writing down a message of coming destruction and then hiding from the king (36:26). Baruch became an important figure in later Jewish tradition, and several writings from centuries after his time were attributed to him, including the book of Baruch found in the Apocrypha (writings included in some Christian Bibles but not in the Hebrew canon). Those later books tell us about how he was remembered, not about the historical man.
cultural:
Scribes in the ancient Near East were part of the educated elite. They served kings, temples, and wealthy households, drafting letters, contracts, and records. The Shaphan family in Jeremiah shows how scribal families could hold power across generations (36:10-12). A scribe of Baruch's training could reasonably hope for a place in the royal administration.

The phrase “your life as a spoil of war” (verse 5) uses a military image that recurs in Jeremiah (21:9, 38:2, 39:18). After a battle, the victors carried off plunder. To have one's life as plunder meant to come out of the disaster with nothing but life itself, as a soldier might escape with only what he could carry. It was a promise of survival, not of prosperity. The lament form of Baruch's complaint (“Woe is me”) was a standard way of expressing grief and protest to God, the same form used in the Psalms and in Jeremiah's own laments (15:10).
literary: This is the shortest chapter in Jeremiah, and it is built with care. The heading (verse 1) ties it to the scroll of chapter 36. God quotes Baruch's own complaint back to him (verse 3), showing that he has heard it. Then the answer sets Baruch's loss beside God's own: Baruch says the LORD has added sorrow to his pain, and God replies that he himself is tearing down what he built and uprooting what he planted (verse 4). These four verbs come from Jeremiah's call (1:10), where God said Jeremiah would uproot and tear down, build and plant. The chapter ends with a pair of contrasts: Baruch seeks great things, God brings great disaster; the whole land is under judgment, but Baruch's life is spared. The repeated verb to seek in verse 5 frames the central question: what is Baruch really looking for?

outline.t: The setting: the year the scroll was written
God's answer: do not seek great things; your life will be spared

doctrines.note: God doesn't dismiss Baruch's grief; he quotes it and answers it. The answer places Baruch's pain inside God's own sorrow over what he is tearing down.
God promises Baruch his life “wherever you go” (verse 5). In a time of national collapse, God's care reaches down to one faithful scribe.
The warning against seeking great things for oneself is a word about human ambition in a time of judgment. Faithfulness, not greatness, is what God asks of his servants.

words.note: Baqash, to seek, to try to obtain. It appears twice in verse 5: do you seek great things for yourself? Stop seeking. The verb can describe seeking God (29:13) or seeking one's own interests. The contrast is between what Baruch wants and what God is doing.

Yagon, sorrow or grief. Baruch complains that the LORD has added sorrow to his pain (verse 3). The word appears in Jeremiah's own lament over his people (8:18) and describes the inner weight of grief.

Menuchah, rest or a place of rest. Baruch says he has found no rest (verse 3). In the Old Testament, rest is often linked to the promised land and God's presence (Deuteronomy 12:9, Psalm 95:11). In a land about to be judged, there was no rest to be found.

Shalal, spoil or plunder taken in war. God promises Baruch his life as spoil (verse 5), meaning he will escape with his life, though perhaps with little else. It is the same promise given to those who surrendered to Babylon (38:2) and to Ebed-melech (39:18).

christ: God answers Baruch's weariness not by removing the burden but by placing it inside his own grief: he too is losing what he built and planted. The Christian confession is that in Jesus God entered human sorrow fully. Jesus wept over Jerusalem as it faced judgment (Luke 19:41), and he taught his followers that the way of discipleship is not seeking greatness for oneself but taking up the cross (Mark 8:34-35, 10:43-45). The link to this chapter is thematic. It shows the same pattern the gospel reveals: God does not promise his servants worldly success, but he promises himself and life that cannot finally be taken away.

hard.q: Is it wrong to want great things? Why does God tell Baruch to stop seeking them?
hard.a: The text doesn't say exactly what the great things were. Some interpreters think Baruch hoped for a high position at court, like his brother Seraiah; others think he hoped for relief, for the prophecies to be reversed, or for a reward for his faithfulness. The warning is set against the backdrop of national judgment: when God is tearing down the whole land, it makes no sense to build a personal empire. Read this way, the chapter isn't a blanket condemnation of ambition but a word about timing and priorities, fitting what Jesus later taught about seeking first the kingdom of God. Others read it more broadly, as a warning against self-seeking in God's service at any time. Both readings agree that God's promise to Baruch was modest but sure: not greatness, but life.

questions: Baruch was exhausted and found no rest. What burdens have left you weary, and what would it mean to hear that God knows your complaint?
God told Baruch not to seek great things for himself. What great things do you seek, and how do they fit with what God is doing in the world?
God promised Baruch only his life, not success. Is that enough? What does it look like to be content with that promise?
